query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 2–3 at.% Mo into the titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy and then applying a thermal aging treatment (700°C for 5 hours) will trigger the formation of finely dispersed nano-scale precipitates that effectively hinder dislocation motion, thereby enhancing the alloy’s yield strength and overall high-temperature mechanical performance compared to the untreated single-phase alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid solution state.
generation.intervention: Add ~2–3 at.% Mo to the alloy composition and subject it to a thermal aging treatment at 700°C for 5 hours to induce precipitation.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing conditions (e.g., tensile or compressive tests conducted around 600–700°C) and extreme-environment exposures where high strength and stability are required.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale precipitates (potentially σ or coherent L12 phases) uniformly dispersed within the matrix that form during the aging treatment.
generation.mechanism: The Mo addition promotes the nucleation and growth of thermally stable precipitates during aging, which act as obstacles to dislocation motion. This precipitation strengthening mechanism enhances yield strength by pinning dislocations and modifying the effective slip channels, improving mechanical performance under high temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-added and aged alloy is predicted to display an approximate 20–30% improvement in yield strength and enhanced high-temperature performance relative to the unmodified alloy. Precise improvement metrics remain uncertain pending detailed kinetic and phase analysis.
generation.baseline: Titanium–nickel-based HEA without Mo addition and without the thermal aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to titanium- and nickel-containing single-phase solid-solution HEAs. It is relevant under elevated-temperature testing regimes (e.g., 600–700°C) and may not extend to drastically different alloy chemistries or temperature ranges without further validation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature, type, and fraction of precipitates (e.g., σ versus L12 phases) that will form, as well as the precise magnitude of the mechanical property enhancement, depend on the alloy’s overall compositional balance and aging kinetics. Further experimental work will be required to optimize the Mo content and thermal aging parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the titanium–nickel HEA. Set A is modified with an addition of ~2–3 at.% Mo followed by thermal aging at 700°C for 5 hours. Set B is the control with no Mo addition or aging treatment. Perform identical elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile tests at 600–700°C) on both sets. Use microstructural characterization techniques (TEM, XRD) to verify precipitate formation.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (size, distribution, and type of precipitates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added and aged alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement (approximately 20% or greater in yield strength) over the control group, or if the expected nano-scale precipitate phase is not observed in the microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Adding Mo to the Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mox (x = 0 and 0.1) alloy strengthens with σ phase. The body-centered cubic (bcc) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) improved the elevated mechanical property and corrosion property at the same time. The present alloys are all BCC solid-solution structures and disperse with the nano B2-type NiAl precipitates in the matrix. Moreover, Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mo0.1 exists as σ phase with rich Cr and Mo contents and a lack of Ni content along the grain boundary. The mechanical properties of the alloys improve upon Mo addition, reaching a yield strength of 413 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 430 MPa, and an elongation of 14.7% at 600 °C. This is ascribed to the slip frustration hardening (SFH) of nano NiAl precipitates and the precipitation hardening of σ phase. The results indicate that Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mo0.1 shows good strength–ductility balance at elevated temperature. Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mo0.1 alloy exhibits superior corrosion resistance compared to Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5 and 304 stainless steel.
